note:
We know from fifteen references in Acts 7–13 that Paul was also called “Saul,” the Hb. name borne by Israel’s first king, who had belonged to the tribe of Benjamin (1 Sam. 9:1, 2), as did the apostle (Phil. 3:5). In his letters, however, he always calls himself “Paul,” a common Roman name, probably connected with his Roman citizenship (Acts 16:37, 38; 22:25–28). Before entering Galatia, Paul had evangelized the proconsul of Cyprus, who bore the same name (Sergius Paulus; Acts 13:9 note).

**apostle.** The word means “messenger.” Paul could on occasion use it to refer to an envoy sent by a church such as Epaphroditus (Phil. 2:25), but he uses it often in Galatians to denote emissaries uniquely sent by the risen Christ and bearing His delegated authority, including the original apostles at Jerusalem (1:17, 19; 1 Cor. 15:9). Paul here identifies himself as an apostle along these latter lines. Paul claims the authority of an apostle to lay the foundation of the church (1 Cor. 3:10; 9:1; 14:37, 38; Eph. 2:20; 3:3–5). His apostleship and calling came directly from God Himself (1:11–2:10). See note on 2 Cor. 1:1.

**not from men nor through man.** Without denying Jesus’ humanity, Paul here implies His divine authority by identifying Him with the Father who raised Him from the dead. Christ directly calls His apostles, without human intermediaries (Luke 6:13; Acts 1:2, 21–26; 9:15). Apparently the Judaizers in Galatia sought to undermine Paul’s gospel by alleging that his authority was derived from the Twelve (vv. 11, 12, 16–20).

Each of Paul’s letters begins with a reference to these two blessings from God. “Grace” translates the Gk. _charis,_ which means “an undeserved act of kindness.” Paul uses this word more often than any other NT writer and gives it immense theological significance. It refers to all that God has given us in Christ, nothing of which we have earned or can repay. “Peace” refers to the relationship that Christ’s death and resurrection (1:4) have established with God for those who believe the gospel. For Paul’s own comments on the meaning of these two terms, see Rom. 5:1, 2.

Only Christ, in His death and resurrection, can deliver the sinner from the order of united human rebellion against God. Believers no longer belong to this age but have been brought by Christ, through the Spirit, into “the age to come” (Eph. 1:21), which Paul will later refer to as the “new creation” (2 Cor. 5:17; Gal. 6:15).

verse_quote: him who called you in the grace.
note: This is not Paul the preacher, but God Himself (Rom. 1:6, 7; 8:28, 30; 1 Pet. 1:15). God’s grace comes to us at His initiative, by His call, and not because of anything we have done to deserve it (1:15; Rom. 4:4–8; 8:30; 9:11–13).

Though the Judaizers may present their message as “gospel,” no teaching that claims that Christ’s redemptive achievement needs to be supplemented by our efforts deserves to be called “good news.”

**some who trouble.** Probably Jewish Christians from Jerusalem who insisted that Gentiles must not only believe in Jesus Christ but also accept circumcision and adhere to other aspects of the ceremonial law in order to become Jews and thereby be saved (2:3–5, 12; 5:4, 5; 6:12, 13). Various shades of this idea were widespread among some early Jewish Christians (Acts 15:1; 21:20, 21; Phil. 3:2, 3).

Those who add any additional requirements for salvation to faith in Jesus Christ, no matter how excellent their credentials, twist the gospel into another form. The preachers of the false gospel are under God’s condemnation.

**1:9 accursed.** Paul’s usual thanksgiving for his readers is here replaced by the threat of a covenant curse, repeated for emphasis. The Gk. word is _anathema_, used also in Rom. 9:3. Paul’s righteous indignation toward anyone who would obscure God’s grace in Christ comes to expression in his later wish that they would emasculate themselves (5:12), which would disqualify them from entering the Lord’s assembly (Deut. 23:1; see Phil. 3:2).

Paul’s opponents in Galatia attacked not only the gospel but also its messenger, Paul. One of their charges was that Paul preached an easy form of the gospel, requiring neither circumcision nor obedience to the Sabbath laws and dietary restrictions, but only faith in Jesus as Messiah (4:10; 5:11).

Paul defends himself against his opponents’ charge that he is in rebellion against the Jerusalem apostles who gave him his authority in the first place, or that his gospel is at odds with theirs. Paul contends that his authority and gospel come from God alone—the Jerusalem apostles merely confirmed those things. This argument extends at least through the end of chapter 1 and perhaps into chapter 2.

Paul’s persecution of the church before his call was well known to the early Christians (Acts 7:58; 8:3; 9:1, 2). Paul himself was profoundly ashamed of this part of his past (1 Cor. 15:9), although he looked on it as evidence that God’s grace can overcome the resistance of even the most rebellious sinners (Acts 22:4, 5; 26:9–11; 1 Cor. 15:10; Phil. 3:6; 1 Tim. 1:13, 14). Paul’s point in this and the following verse is that he did not derive his gospel from his pre-converted life in Judaism.

Paul is fond of pointing out to opponents like those in Galatia that being a Jew, even a zealous Jew, is insufficient for salvation. Paul considers his own experience proof that zeal for the law will not save (Rom. 9:30–10:4; 2 Cor. 11:22; Phil. 3:4–6).

Paul consciously echoes the call of Jeremiah (Jer. 1:5) and, perhaps, the servant spoken of by Isaiah (Is. 49:1, 5), whose prophecies spoke of the progress of the gospel to the Gentiles. Paul is conscious that his apostleship (v. 1 note) is in continuity with the OT prophetic tradition (see Rom. 15:8–12).

**called me by his grace.** See note on v. 3; theological note “Effectual Calling” on p. 2146. Paul’s call to be an apostle, like the faith of every believer, is the product of God’s prior grace. Before birth, and therefore before they could do anything good or bad, God chose to create faith in His elect (Rom. 9:10–13; Eph. 1:4–6). No one can earn God’s call; it is a free gift.

Both “nations” and “Gentiles” are correct translations of the Gk. word used here. Jewish writers used the term to refer to everyone that was not a Jew. Paul was called to preach to the Gentiles (2:9; Acts 9:15; 22:21; 26:17; Rom. 1:5; 15:16), but he did not regard this as a call to preach exclusively to Gentiles. In Acts 13–28, he frequently preaches to Jews, and such passages as Rom. 1:14–16; 9:1–5; 1 Cor. 9:20 show that he was ready to evangelize Jews when the opportunity presented itself.

**consult with anyone.** Paul did, of course, meet with Ananias three days after his conversion (Acts 9:10–19; 22:12–16). The word translated “consult,” however, suggests laying something before someone or submitting it for comment and approval. Paul certainly did not consult Ananias in this sense. Ananias’s role was to confirm Paul’s calling to preach to the Gentiles and to baptize him.

Paul’s conversion and call took place near Damascus (Acts 9:3; 22:6; 26:12). He spent several days in the city after his conversion (Acts 9:19). This ancient city is on a fertile plain between two rivers, and the traveler from there must literally “go up” to Jerusalem in the Palestinian highlands. Jerusalem was the cultural and religious center of Palestine, and home to James, Peter, and John, who are prominent in Acts and Galatians as leaders of the early Christian community in Jerusalem (2:9). Paul stresses that his call to preach to the Gentiles came from God and not from the leaders of the Jerusalem church. Arabia was ruled by a Nabatean king, Aretas IV, who struggled with Rome for control of Damascus. When Paul was converted, Aretas’s governor was in control of the city and apparently aided angry Jews in an effort to kill Paul (Acts 9:23–25; 2 Cor. 11:32, 33).

The “many days” of Acts 9:23.

**to Jerusalem.** Paul’s first trip to Jerusalem after his conversion (Acts 9:26–30).

**visit.** This translates a Gk. word that means visiting someone for the purpose of getting information. Paul may have interviewed Peter about Jesus’ life and teaching.

**Cephas.** Peter’s Aramaic name was “Cephas.” Both “Cephas” and “Peter” mean “rock.”

See Matt. 13:55 and Mark 6:3. This James is not the disciple James (son of Zebedee) who is frequently coupled with Peter and John in the Gospels. Herod Agrippa murdered that James in the church’s earliest days (Acts 12:2). Nor is he James the son of Alphaeus (Matt. 10:3). James, the Lord’s brother, at first did not believe in Jesus (John 7:5) but later was converted, perhaps as a result of seeing the risen Lord (1 Cor. 15:7). He emerged as a recognized leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 12:17; 15:13–21; 21:18–26).

See Acts 9:30. Paul returned home to Tarsus (Acts 9:11; 21:39; 22:3), the most important city in Cilicia. This part of Cilicia was under the administration of the Roman province of Syria during the early first century. Paul’s use of the two names is accurate.
Paul could be referring to the specific region of OT Judah, or to the Roman province of Judea, which included ancient Judah, Samaria, and Galilee.

Either after his conversion or, more likely, after his first visit to Jerusalem.

**again to Jerusalem.** This may refer to a second visit after his conversion, or to a third visit, recorded in Acts 15:2. The purpose of the visit mentioned here corresponds well with the purpose of the visit in Acts 15, but it is difficult then to explain why Paul leaves the second visit (Acts 11:27–30) out of his narrative. If, as some scholars believe, Galatians was written after Paul’s first missionary journey (Acts 13; 14) but before the Jerusalem council (Acts 15), then the journey spoken of here is the Acts 11 journey, and the Acts 15 journey had not yet occurred when the apostle wrote to the church at Galatia. Some object to this theory on the grounds that vv. 7–9 assume that Paul’s Gentile ministry has already begun. Paul does not seem to have begun his missionary travels at the time of the Acts 11 journey (Acts 13:1–3), although he and Barnabas had been teaching Gentiles (Acts 11:20–26) when the church in Syrian Antioch sent them to Jerusalem with an offering for the poor. Some scholars believe that the evidence favors understanding this private meeting with three “pillars” (2:2, 6–9) as another account of the more public council of apostles and elders that Luke records in Acts 15. Others hold that the interview recorded in Gal. 2:1–10 took place quietly when Barnabas and Paul delivered the donation from the church in Antioch to the elders in Jerusalem (Acts 11:27–30), and that the Jerusalem council had not yet occurred when Paul wrote Galatians.

**Barnabas.** A native of Cyprus and one of the earliest Christians (Acts 4:36). Barnabas’s name in Aramaic means “son of encouragement,” and his appearances in Acts demonstrate that he lived up to his name (Acts 4:36, 37; 11:22–24, 30).

**Titus.** Although not mentioned in Acts, Titus was one of Paul’s most trusted companions and messengers, tasked with the delicate challenge of effecting reconciliation between the Corinthian church and Paul, with fiscal stewardship, and with establishing order in the churches on the Mediterranean island of Crete. Cf. 2 Cor. 2:12, 13; 7:6; 8:6; Titus 1:4, 5. Since he was not circumcised (v. 3), Titus was obviously a Gentile who had not become a full proselyte to Judaism prior to his conversion to Christianity, although he might have been a “God fearer” before coming to faith in Christ (Acts 10:2 note).

If this is the Acts 11 visit, the revelation may have been the prophecy of Agabus (11:28). If not, it was probably similar to other special revelations that Paul received from God (Acts 9:4–6; 16:9; 18:9, 10; 2 Cor. 12:1–6). If the meeting described here is the council of Acts 15, apparently Paul’s special revelation confirmed the decision of the church at Antioch that the dispute over the Gentiles’ status must be referred to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem (Acts 15:2).

**in vain.** While the Jerusalem leaders were not the source of Paul’s authority, his efforts to preach the gospel among the Gentiles would have been hindered if these influential men had opposed him.

See 5:12 and Acts 15:1. Circumcision was the distinguishing mark of the Jew, and the final step in the conversion of a male Gentile to the Jewish religion. Some Jewish Christians believed that Gentiles also had to accept circumcision in order to be saved and to be counted as belonging to God’s chosen people. Paul is vehemently opposed to this teaching and maintains throughout Galatians that justification is by faith in Christ alone, and not at all by works.

Paul considered the doctrine of justification by grace alone through faith alone to be so important that he excluded from the church all who did not hold to it (1:8, 9; 5:2–4). Those who teach that justification is not by faith alone have been cut off from Christ (5:4).

**freedom.** The freedom of the believer is not freedom to sin, but freedom from the curse the law pronounces on sin (3:10–14; 5:1, 13). In this context, Paul also has in view believers’ freedom, under the new covenant, from aspects of the law of Moses such as circumcision and the dietary laws, which set ancient Israel apart from the nations.

**slavery.** Probably bondage to sin (Rom. 6:15–23; 7:25) and to the curse that the law pronounces on those who violate it (3:10). By placing excessive obligations on Christians’ consciences and making assurance of God’s favor contingent on one’s own performance, the opponents of the gospel actually imposed an unbearable yoke on believers (4:8–10; 5:1; cf. Acts 15:10, 11). Outside of Jesus Christ, there is only spiritual slavery and bondage.

See v. 14; 1:8, 9 and notes. The declaration of the sinner as righteous in God’s sight comes only through the faith that is graciously given to the believer by God (1:6, 15; Eph. 2:8). Any attempt to add to the work of Christ that alone justifies us, such as circumcision, is a denial of the sufficiency of faith in Christ’s merits for satisfying God’s justice, and therefore is a perversion of the gospel.
Just as the external mark of circumcision does not define the boundary of God’s people, so worldly prestige is not important to God (Deut. 10:17; 1 Sam. 16:7; Rom. 2:25–29).

See note on 1:16. Paul describes himself as “an apostle to the Gentiles” (Rom. 11:13) and marvels at the calling he has received by grace to disclose the “mystery” that the Gentiles now share in Israel’s covenantal privileges (Eph. 3:1–6).

**Peter ... circumcised.** Peter was apparently the chief spokesman of the early Jerusalem church (Acts 1–12). Only with great reluctance did he respond to God’s command to associate with the Gentile Cornelius (Acts 10). Although Peter recognized the necessity of including Gentiles in God’s people (Acts 10:34, 35; 11:17; 15:7–11), God called him primarily to preach the gospel to Jews.

See notes on v. 7; cf. 1:18, 19. These three men had special authority in the early Jerusalem church. Peter and John are frequently seen together (Acts 3; 4), and James (1:19 note) was prominent in the Jerusalem church (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18). “Pillars” was used as a metaphor for people in important leadership positions.

**grace ... given to me.** Regarding Paul’s conversion and call, see 1:15 and note. Paul frequently referred to his call as God’s grace, given to him (Rom. 1:5; 12:3; 15:15, 16; 1 Cor. 3:10).

**we should go to the Gentiles.** Barnabas, like Paul, was chiefly a missionary to the Gentiles (Acts 13; 14; 15:36–41).

Some associate these words with the purpose of Paul’s second visit to Jerusalem (Acts 11:27–30). On that visit, Paul and Barnabas were commissioned to take an offering from Antioch to the Christians in Judea who were suffering because of a famine. In this case, the poverty of which Paul speaks is literal poverty. Others believe that these words refer to Paul’s collection for the Jerusalem saints (Acts 24:17; Rom. 15:26; 1 Cor. 16:1–3; 2 Cor. 8; 9), to which the Galatians contributed (1 Cor. 16:1), but that interpretation is unlikely.

The capital of the Roman province of Syria and the largest city of that province. Antioch was home to a large Jewish community and, not surprisingly, was the first place mentioned in Acts where Jewish Christians preached the gospel to Gentiles (Acts 11:19, 20). Not only was the church at Antioch the first church in our records to bring Jewish and Gentile Christians together in worship and fellowship; but also, as far as we know, it was the first church to send missionaries to other regions, to preach the gospel specifically to Gentiles (Acts 13:1–3).

Both Peter and Barnabas (v. 13) succumbed to pressure from a group that believed that to be circumcised—that is, to become a full Jewish proselyte—was necessary in order to be saved and to be regarded as a Christian. Peter evidently had come under criticism for sharing meals with uncircumcised Gentiles after preaching the gospel to the Roman centurion Cornelius and his circle of relatives and friends (Acts 11:1–3).

See note on v. 5.

**live like a Gentile.** Before the arrival of the “circumcision” group, Peter had eaten freely with Gentiles, apparently disregarding the Mosaic regulations concerning kosher and non-kosher foods (v. 12). After the circumcision party arrived, Peter was acting as if Gentiles had to become Jews in order to be saved and to become full members of God’s people. These actions were inconsistent with his former practice and belief that Gentiles did not have to become Jews in order to be saved.

These verses are central in Galatians, and quite possibly are the epistle’s “thesis statement.” Paul’s point is that everyone (circumcised Jew as well as uncircumcised Gentile) is placed in a right relationship with God through faith in Jesus Christ alone. The words “righteousness,” “righteous,” “justify,” and “justification” in the NT are all from the same Gk. root and have related meanings. In these two verses, the term “justify” appears three times; three times it is said to be by faith (believing) in Christ, and three times “the works of the law” are excluded as the means of justification.

**2:16** See theological note “Faith and Works” on p. 2231. In the OT, God rules and judges with perfect justice (1 Sam. 26:23), and pronounces His verdict of innocence or guilt. To “justify” is to declare to be right (Deut. 25:1). But if no one living is righteous before God (Ps. 143:2), how can there be hope of that verdict (Job 9:2)? As God is the Judge, whose verdict is final and just, so He is the Savior who can provide deliverance from His own judgment (Jon. 2:9). God’s righteousness is revealed not only as His requirement, but also as His gift (Is. 45:24, 25; 54:14–17). That gift comes at last through the Messiah (Is. 53:8; Jer. 23:5, 6; 33:14–16). Paul proclaims the fulfillment of the OT promise (Rom. 3:21–26). Faith receives the gift of Christ’s righteousness, a gift that includes forgiveness through His atonement.

**works of the law.** Paul has been referring to the “works” that distinguish Jews from Gentiles (v. 15), such as circumcision, dietary restrictions, and Sabbath-keeping. His phrase, however, includes all the efforts of fallen humanity to keep God’s law so as to merit His justifying verdict (cf. Eph. 2:8, 9; Titus 3:4–8).

**no one will be justified.** A near quotation of Ps. 143:2. Our legal observances cannot establish a right relationship with God. Something other than our law-keeping is needed for that, and God has provided it in the gift of Christ’s righteousness—His perfect obedience to the law and His atoning death on the cross. Faith does not _merit_ God’s acceptance; it _accepts_ Christ’s merit before God (Phil. 3:9).

The Galatian agitators and the “men ... from James” (v. 12) considered Paul (and Peter) a “sinner” (like the Gentiles of v. 15) for breaking the Jewish dietary food laws. They probably also accused Paul’s gospel of promoting sin (Rom. 3:8).

The Gk. word translated “tore down” is used in the NT to mean the tearing down of an edifice (Matt. 24:2; Mark 13:2; Luke 21:6; Rom. 14:20). Paul may be thinking here of efforts to keep God’s commands in order to merit justification from Him, or perhaps the maintenance of regulations that mark the boundary between law-abiding Jewish “insiders” and lawless Gentiles outside (Eph. 2:14, 15). To rebuild the wall of the law, in this sense, is to bring in again the condemnation of the law. The lawbreaker is not the one who turns from the law to Christ for justification; it is the one who turns back again from Christ to the law for his justification.

Paul died to the law in the death of Christ; he was crucified with Christ (v. 20), for he was united to Christ, who died in his place (3:13; Rom. 4:25; 5:6). So, too, he was raised with Christ and reconciled to God (Col. 2:12; 3:1). Death to the law does not violate the law, for Christ met the law’s demands on the believer’s behalf. It is therefore “through the law” that believers are released from the bondage and condemnation of the law. Believers, however, are not released from the obligation to follow God’s law as their guide to what pleases God in their sanctification (Gal. 5:14; 6:2). See theological note “The Threefold Use of the Law” on p. 273.

Union with Christ means that He represented us in His death and resurrection. But it means more, for it is a living union. Jesus is present with the believer; by the Spirit, the Lord lives in inward fellowship with His own. Paul does not mean that the individuality of a person is suppressed or absorbed; he lives “in the flesh” by “faith.” The union is a spiritual relationship of the utmost intimacy.
Christ was placed before the Galatians’ in Paul’s preaching, which they heard with faith (v. 2).
Paul appeals to the Galatians’ own experience of the Holy Spirit to prove that one’s keeping of the law is not necessary for his justification or for becoming a Christian (Acts 10:47; 11:17; 15:8).

Perhaps Paul has in mind not simply attempting to keep the law without the Spirit (Rom. 7:7–25) but also the attempting to gain favor with God by cutting the flesh in circumcision (6:13; Rom. 2:28, 29; Phil. 3:2, 3). In either case, Paul warns his readers against the attempt to win justification by performing some work. Justification comes only through God’s grace by faith in Jesus Christ alone (2:16).

Abraham was the father of the Jews and the person with whom God first established circumcision as a covenantal sign (Gen. 17:10). Even this revered patriarch was placed in a right relationship with God by faith (Paul cites Gen. 15:6), long before he was circumcised (Rom. 4:11). Paul reverses his opponents’ charge that he is undercutting God’s covenant with Abraham. The true children of Abraham share his faith, regardless of whether they are physically descended from him. The promise to Abraham is also a promise of blessing to the Gentiles, a blessing that is received only through a faith like Abraham’s.

Paul’s point is that no sinner can keep the law in its entirety, so anyone who depends on his personal observance of the law stands under the law’s curse. He supports his point by quoting Deut. 27:26. After the passage from which Paul quotes, Deuteronomy lists the curses that would fall upon Israel for disobedience. Most Jews of Paul’s day realized that Israel had broken the law and had received the curses that were threatened, most painfully in the exile (Deut. 28:15–30:20; cf. Acts 15:10).

Paul now cites Hab. 2:4 as Scripture’s announcement of the only means for sinners to receive righteousness and life. Paul cites this OT text in Rom. 1:17, making it virtually the theme passage for his unfolding of the gospel, which is God’s power for salvation to both Jew and Gentile (Rom. 1–8). See theological note “Justification by Faith.”

verse_quote: the law is not of faith.
note: Here Paul speaks of the law as God’s requirement apart from the promise of God’s covenant of grace. Leviticus states the requirement for all those who seek to be justified by the works of the law—perfect obedience—and predicts the failure and curse that would follow (Lev. 18:5; 26:14–38). The promise of grace is also repeated (Lev. 26:40–45), for it is not voided by the law’s demands or Israel’s failure to keep them (3:15–22).

Since we have violated the law, we deserve to receive the law’s curse and God’s condemnation. But Christ bore the law’s curse in our place, giving us peace with God (Rom. 3:21–26; 4:25; 5:1–8; 2 Cor. 5:21; Col. 2:13–15; cf. Mark 10:45; John 1:29; 1 Pet. 2:24). See theological note “Atonement” on p. 1983.

**“Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.”** The law’s requirement that the body of a flagrant violator be suspended from a tree (Deut. 21:23; cf. Acts 5:30; 10:39; 13:29; 1 Pet. 2:24), signaling God’s utter rejection, was fulfilled in the form of Jesus’ execution, Roman crucifixion. Before his conversion, Paul may have viewed this as disproving the claim that Jesus is God’s Messiah, believing that Jesus was cursed for what He had done and thus not qualified to be the Savior. Having been converted and seeing the truth of the cross, He affirms that the curse Christ bore was not His own but ours.

Cf. v. 8; Gen 12:3; theological note “Jesus Christ as Mediator” on p. 2157. Believing Gentiles, whose lives are marked by the indwelling Spirit, fulfill the promise that through Abraham all nations would be blessed. The Spirit is the blessing promised to Abraham.

God promised saving blessing to the nations through Abraham “and his offspring”—Christ, descended from Abraham according to His human nature. That covenant promise was not canceled by the later giving of the law through Moses. The law does not oppose the promises (v. 21) but assumes them. The Mosaic administration shows the hopelessness of earning salvation and points God’s people to faith in Christ (v. 24).

Paul is well aware that the noun “offspring” in the singular may be collective as well as individual (v. 29; Rom. 4:18). He is affirming that Christ is the Seed (descendant) to whom the promise finally refers, so others become Abraham’s seed by virtue of their union with Christ through faith. See theological note “Covenant” on p. 37. To call Christ Abraham’s “seed” is another way of calling Him the true Israel.

In Ex. 12:40, this figure is given for the length of Israel’s stay in Egypt. In the Septuagint version of Exodus, the time of the patriarchs’ stay in Canaan is included in the 430 years. But Paul is not necessarily following the Septuagint in alluding to the passage. It is enough for his purpose to show that centuries passed before the law was given at Sinai (cf. Gen. 15:13; Acts 7:6).

Probably in order to define sin specifically as the violation of God’s explicitly stated will, and so to make sin that much worse (Rom. 5:13, 20; 7:7, 8).

**offspring.** In Gen. 17:19, God promises Abraham a son, Isaac, and says He will establish a covenant with Isaac and his “offspring.” Paul regards this use of a singular noun as a pointer to Jesus.

**through angels.** Cf. Deut. 33:2; Acts 7:53; Heb. 2:2.

Moses mediated between God and Israel when God made His covenant with Israel at Mount Sinai (Ex. 19–34). The promise given to Abraham, however, required a mediator who is not merely human and therefore takes precedence over the covenant at Sinai.

**God is one.** Cf. Deut. 6:4. God’s covenant with Abraham, because it did not involve a merely human mediator, demonstrates God’s unity and sovereignty more perfectly than the covenant at Sinai. The fulfillment of God’s covenant with Abraham by the inclusion of the Gentiles in the people of God also demonstrates the unity of God more clearly than the Sinai covenant because it shows His sovereignty over all creation (Rom. 3:29, 30). Paul may also be implying that through the incarnation, obedience, sacrifice, and resurrection of Christ, who is God the Son, the triune God has fulfilled all the conditions for believers to receive the blessings promised to Abraham.

Humanity’s inability to keep the law, not the law itself, is the source of humanity’s broken relationship with God (see Rom. 7:7–25; 8:3).

**contrary to the promises of God.** Paul strongly denies this mistaken conclusion from his argument. The law could be in competition with the gospel only if it could impart life by delivering sinners from its own condemnation. Although the law is good and shows what is pleasing to God (Lev. 18:5; Rom. 7:10), it is not able to give and was never designed to give life to lawbreakers (2 Cor. 3:6). Jews, who possessed the law and looked to its commands to be justified, were condemned by it. Scripture takes full account of this, showing that all are condemned sinners and pointing to the need for the promised Savior.

A “guardian” was a slave responsible for a child’s training, especially for pointing out and punishing misbehavior (see 4:1, 2). Like a guardian, the law pointed out sin and punished it. Another important function of guardians was to separate and protect the child from the influence of outsiders. The law functioned in a similar way to separate Israel from the Gentiles. That function of the ceremonial law has also ended. See theological note “The Law of God” on p. 124.

verse_quote: you are all sons of God.
note: We are adopted “sons” because we are united to the true Son, Jesus Christ. Baptism seals that union with Christ. It is a vital union, for Christ lives in us (2:20). It is also a representative union; Christ died and lives for us (Rom. 6:5–11). To be clothed with Christ implies both that His righteousness is our covering and that we are a new creation in Christ (Rom. 13:14; Eph. 4:24; Col. 3:10).

verse_quote: you are all one in Christ Jesus.
note: The wall of separation between Jew and Gentile is removed for those united to Christ: all in Christ are Abraham’s seed (Eph. 2:14–16; Col. 3:11). Indeed, no human distinctions avail as advantages in the matter of salvation. Paul does not obliterate these distinctions, such as those between the sexes, but indicates that they give no preferential status in terms of our union with Christ and of our sharing in his saving benefits. Until Christ returns, the created order remains, and order in the church takes account of it (1 Cor. 11:3; 14:34; 1 Tim. 2:11–14). See theological note “The Church” on p. 2094.

In the ancient world, inheritance passed from fathers to sons, so sonship entailed the privileges of being heirs (4:7). Thus, for females as well as males (and slaves as well as free persons), to be “sons of God” in Christ Jesus (vv. 26, 28) entails their inclusion among the heirs of the blessings promised to Abraham, specifically the life-giving presence of the Holy Spirit (v. 14). Here, those who believe and are identified with Christ are “Abraham’s seed”—that is, true Israel—because Christ is “Abraham’s seed.”

Paul has compared the law to a prison warden (3:23) and a guardian (3:24 note). Now he compares its preparatory role to that of a guardian or trustee of a minor. The full right reserved for one who has grown up is adoption as a son and the receiving of the inheritance.

The Gk. phrase in contemporary literature outside the NT refers to the basic elements that make up the world—earth, wind, water, and fire, according to ancient thought. Here Paul is probably applying this concept to the law and especially its elaborate and outward ceremonies and ordinances, as suited to God’s people in the old age. Relative to the freedom to come (v. 4), life under the Mosaic law was a kind of bondage (cf. Col. 2:8, 20–22). In v. 9, Paul uses the same term to refer to the idolatrous practices in the Galatians’ pagan past, drawing an implicit and shocking link between the Judaizers’ misuse of God’s law and the pagans’ allegiance to false deities.

The time set by the Father (v. 2), “the end of the ages” (1 Cor. 10:11), when the promises of God are realized in Christ.

**God sent forth his Son.** His eternal Son, sent to be born of a woman. Thus, Paul assumes the preincarnate existence and intrinsic deity of Christ.

**under the law.** Although Christ was without sin (2 Cor. 5:21), He was born under the law, not only as one obligated to fulfill it, but also as one identified with sinners who are under the curse of the law. His death freed us from that curse (3:10–14), and His perfect obedience is the ground of our being declared righteous (Rom. 5:15–21; 2 Cor. 5:21; Phil. 3:9; Heb. 10:5–10).

The concept of redemption comes from the institution of slavery. In both the Jewish and Greco-Roman worlds, a slave could buy his freedom (or someone else could buy it for him) by paying a redemption price to his owners. The price of our redemption was paid by the Father in the blood of His Son (1 Pet. 1:17–19), and by the Son in giving His life a ransom for many (Matt. 20:28). By this, God paid the ransom price to Himself.

**those ... under the law.** Not only Jews, circumcised under the law of Moses, but also Gentiles, for both are under the curse of God’s law in Adam (3:13, 14; cf. Rom. 5:12–21).

**adoption as sons.** Paul has been speaking of God’s people under the law as His sons, but sons with no greater privileges than those of slaves (vv. 1, 2; cf. Ex. 4:23; Is. 1:2; Hos. 11:1). Why was Israel called “sons”? Probably because they were identified with Adam, God’s first son (e.g., Luke 3:38), in his task to subdue the earth and reflect God’s glory throughout the earth (Gen. 1:28; on the passing on of this commission to Israel; cf. Gen. 28:14 in Is. 54:3; Ex. 1:7, 12, 20; 19:5, 6). Both Adam and Israel were disobedient sons, but Christ, as the last Adam and true Israel, was God’s faithful Son. Paul now describes the only way in which the sons become full members of the household, no longer minors but fully adopted children with all the privileges that come with being heirs of the Lord’s promise. God seals our adoption by giving us the Spirit of His Son (Rom. 8:9–17). Paul, then, is speaking here particularly of the privilege that belongs to believers under the new covenant. Christ was “declared to be the Son of God in power” (Rom. 1:4), so those who trust in Him and come into union with Him through His Spirit share in that identity. But since Christ is God’s Son not only functionally (as Adam and Israel were to be) but also ontologically (i.e., He is the divine Son), believers can only be identified with His functional sonship by adoption, not by original kinship.

The Aramaic word for “Father,” used by Jesus (Mark 14:36). It was natural for Jesus, God’s Son in a unique sense, to use this term. Now the Spirit puts the same word on the lips of men and women who are adopted in Christ (Rom. 8:15).

Their knowledge of God was not the result of their own inquiry, but the sovereign work of the one who opened their understanding (see 1 Cor. 8:3; 13:12). See theological note “Knowledge of Self and Knowledge of God” on p. 1278.

**turn back again.** Amazingly, Paul likens the bondage of ceremonial legalism to the bondage of pagan superstition. To accept circumcision as necessary for salvation is to turn back from the liberty of grace to the bondage of the world with its times and seasons (v. 10; Col. 2:8, 20–22), whether those times are Jewish or Gentile.

**weak ... elementary principles.** Before their conversion, the Galatians were subject to the “principles” of a pagan world: its false gods, its astrology, and its seasonal rituals (v. 3 note).

Paul seems to be referring to the observance of Jewish annual festivals. The Jewish agitators among the Galatians probably required not only circumcision for salvation but also adoption of the whole law, including the food laws and religious festivals.

verse_quote: become as I am, for I also have become as you are.
note:
In order to bring the gospel to the Gentile Galatians, Paul had to leave behind the legal restrictions of the Mosaic ceremonial law that were understood to forbid Jewish interaction with Gentiles (1 Cor. 9:19–23). Paul became like the Galatians in freedom from the Mosaic law, and he now encourages them to be like him in freedom from the law insofar as it is understood as an instrument of justification.

**You did me no wrong.** Paul’s positive characterization of his previous relationship with the Galatian Christians (developed further in vv. 13–16) contains an implicit plea for good relations to continue. Paul’s depth of concern for the Galatians is evident throughout this section.

It is not known from what Paul suffered. Eye difficulties (v. 15; 6:11), as well as malaria and epilepsy, have been suggested. There may or may not be a connection with Paul’s “thorn ... in the flesh” (2 Cor. 12:7). It apparently was visible to others and could have tempted them to find his presence offensive or despicable—a temptation that the Galatians had resisted (v. 14). Paul’s illness apparently made him stay longer in Galatia, where he had continuing opportunities to minister.

See 6:12. The source of their zeal may have been a desire to avoid persecution, perhaps by Jewish nationalists who were not Christians and who saw the ethnic inclusiveness of the Christian movement as a threat to their cause.

A touching witness to the depth of Paul’s feeling for those whom he brought to faith in Christ. Paul’s anger in this epistle (1:6, 9; 3:1; 5:12) reflects not only the seriousness with which he regards the task of preserving the truth of the gospel, but also the love that he had for his “children” in Christ., 20
The older son Ishmael was born to Hagar (Gen. 16); the younger son Isaac to Sarah (Gen. 21:1–6). Hagar was Sarah’s slave.

Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar, was born after Abraham and Sarah despaired of having the son God had promised. His birth was “according to the flesh” because Hagar was fertile and of childbearing age when Sarah gave her to Abraham. Thus, Ishmael’s conception, though unusual in view of Abraham’s age, resulted from natural reproductive capacities. Isaac, on the other hand, was born to Sarah by a miracle long after her childbearing years had ended (Gen. 11:30; 17:17; Rom. 4:18–21). God showed that none of His promises are empty (Gen. 18:14; Luke 1:37).

The word may also be translated “figuratively,” but in any case Paul is not speaking of an allegory as we understand the term today, for his use of the imagery is not disconnected from the original context and events that he describes. Paul draws a spiritual lesson from these historical figures and events: the heirs of the blessings promised to Abraham are born through the life-imparting power of God’s Spirit, not through human effort. Hagar and Sarah foreshadowed earthly, unbelieving Jerusalem and the heavenly Jerusalem, respectively, as the following verses reveal. Hagar is a fitting representative of unbelieving Jerusalem because her son, Ishmael, was born as the result of human effort (Gen. 16), and the citizens of unbelieving Jerusalem seek to be justified by their works. Sarah is a fitting representative of believing Jerusalem—“Jerusalem above” (v. 26)—because her son, Isaac, was born as the result of trusting in God’s promise (Gen. 17:15–21; 21:1–7), and the citizens of believing Jerusalem trust only in God’s promises through Christ for their justification.

The place where God established His covenant with Israel (Ex. 19–34).

**corresponds to the present Jerusalem.** In both Paul’s day and our own, most Jews remain, like all unbelievers, in slavery to sin and under the law’s curse revealed at Sinai.

Jerusalem was the city where God had set His name, the place of His dwelling in the midst of His people (Ps. 78:68, 69). The reality of God’s dwelling with us was accomplished in Christ, the true temple (John 2:19). The true Jerusalem is in heaven where He is (Heb. 12:22; Rev. 21:2).

verse_quote: him [Isaac] who was born according to the Spirit.
note: This may be the only explicit passage in the NT that affirms that regeneration of OT believers came through the work of God’s Spirit.

verse_quote: Cast out the slave woman and her son.
note:
The words are Sarah’s (Gen. 21:10), but confirmed by the Lord (Gen. 21:12, 13). Paul cites them as “Scripture” to show that, even as early as the Genesis narrative about Abraham, the decisive factor for blessing was not biological descent or any other natural factor, but faith in God’s promise and His Spirit’s life-imparting power.

**the free woman.** We are not slaves to sin or under the curse of the law (Rom. 6:1–7:6).

Jewish literature of the time compares the law to a yoke to which the obedient submit. Paul does not want his Gentile readers to let the law as a means of justification take the place of Christ in their lives (Matt. 11:29; Acts 15:10).

Regarding both Christ and circumcision as necessary for justification is the same as denying the sufficiency of Christ’s death for justification. For those set free in Christ, to be circumcised for justification is to undertake to do what they cannot do and to reject what Christ has done for them (2:21). It is to return again to the dominion of sin and the law’s curse.

verse_quote: obligated to keep the whole law.
note: To receive circumcision in the belief that one’s standing before God depends on it is to shift one’s dependence from Christ’s perfect righteousness and atoning death to one’s own efforts at law observance. On that basis, nothing less than flawless compliance will avoid the law’s curse (3:10, 12).

That is, they would be renouncing God’s grace by no longer relying on it. Those who are chosen in Christ will be kept from such a renunciation of the gospel (Rom. 8:28–30), and Paul continues to have confidence that his warning will be heeded by the Galatians (v. 10). There may be those, however, who appear to us to be true members of Christ but who later abandon the gospel because they never actually believed the gospel (Rom. 11:22; 1 John 2:19). Scripture admonishes us, therefore, to be “diligent to make your calling and election sure” (2 Pet. 1:10) by living in a way that demonstrates the reality of the Spirit’s presence within us (5:16–6:10; Heb. 10:26, 27; 2 Pet. 1:5–11).

verse_quote: by faith ... the hope of righteousness.
note: The sure hope that attends the righteousness by faith is in contrast to the vain hope that attends the righteousness by legal works. The Holy Spirit gives eager anticipation of our hope in Christ on the last day because we have already been justified in Christ (Rom. 5:1–5, 9, 10). That same Spirit, imparting to us the saving benefits of our risen Savior, is our foretaste of the fulfilled heritage in glory (2 Cor. 5:5; Eph. 1:13).

Paul is not arguing against circumcision in and of itself (6:15; cf. Acts 16:3; 1 Cor. 7:19) but against the attempt to make the rite a requirement for justification.

**faith working through love.** Faith stands in contrast to “works” because it entails directing our dependence away from our actions to rest in the completed work of Christ (Eph. 2:8, 9). Yet genuine faith in Christ does not leave the believer’s affections, motives, and consequent actions unchanged. Saving faith “is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces” (Westminster Confession 11.2). The one who believes in Jesus Christ will demonstrate the reality of his belief through a sanctified life. See theological note “Faith and Works” on p. 2231.
Paul uses the same maxim and imagery to characterize the infectious danger of licentiousness (1 Cor. 5:6) and, here, of legalism (Matt. 16:6).

Paul may be referring to his life before his conversion, or he may be refuting a false charge from his opponents that he preaches the necessity of circumcision for salvation when the Jerusalem apostles are present but leaves out that requirement when in the company of Gentiles (1:10).

**offense of the cross.** See 1 Cor. 1:18–2:5. The cross’s offense was and is its demonstration that no other remedy—nothing that sinful people could contribute—can reconcile us to God. It shatters human pride and self-reliance.

Paul’s righteous anger is a result of seeing young believers led astray (1:9). Emasculation would disqualify those Judaizers from participating in Israel’s worship (Deut. 23:1). Accordingly, if the false teachers remain tenacious in their error, then they are and will be excluded from true worship of Christ and God, and will thus be excluded from the community where salvation is experienced. Jesus had some equally strong words of warning for those who dared to lead others into error (Luke 17:1, 2).
Christian liberty is freedom _from_ sin, not license _to_ sin (Rom. 6:1–7:6). See theological note “Free Will” on p. 1293.

Paul’s letter to the Galatians does not nullify the law. Christ fulfilled the law; He did not abolish it (Matt. 5:17). Certain provisions of the law such as its dietary requirements are no longer applicable to believers under the new covenant, but the Ten Commandments remain as declarations of God’s will for Christian behavior and reflect God’s eternal moral law (Rom. 8:2–8; 13:8–10). Jesus Himself cited Lev. 19:18, which Paul quotes here, as the second great commandment on which all the Law and Prophets depend (Matt. 22:37–39).

**love.** Paul does not set “law” against “love.” In fact, we do not properly love God or neighbor apart from keeping the commands of God’s law. See Rom. 13:10; 1 Cor. 13; cf. Matt. 19:19.

Ironically, the pursuit of justification through commandment-keeping advocated by the Judaizers was producing competition, conflict, conceit, and envy (v. 26) in the Galatians’ relationships with one another—a direct contradiction of the love of neighbor that fulfills the whole law (v. 14).

The Holy Spirit’s dwelling within the believer is a sign that the believer is part of God’s people and an heir of the covenant promises given to Abraham (3:14; 4:6; 5:5). The Spirit’s presence is also a sign that on the final day, God will consummate the blessings that belong to the believer in Christ, and we will then experience them in all their fullness (5:5; cf. 2 Cor. 1:22; 5:5).

See theological note “The Holy Spirit as Sanctifier” on p. 2023. Paul says in 6:13 that the agitators in Galatia wanted to circumcise the Galatians in order to glory in their “flesh.” Paul uses the word “flesh” in at least three ways. The broadest use is a simple reference to humanness. Another use is for the physical body. The narrowest use, especially when placed in contrast to “Spirit,” is to refer to the sinful human nature that is part of the old fallen world, which here includes the mind and soul. If the Galatians abandon Christ and place their confidence in the law, they will be turning back to reliance on the flesh, and thus to existence under the law’s curse. It would mean that they are not a part of the “new creation” (6:15) and have not been “delivered out of this present evil age” (1:4).

There is hope as well as warning in Paul’s words. Although the desires of the flesh oppose the Spirit, the desires given by the Holy Spirit prove that we are no longer in bondage to the flesh. Only believers—in whom the Spirit dwells and whose lives the Spirit governs (5:18)—experience conviction by Spirit as a result of this conflict. The presence of this opposition and conviction about it in the believer’s life assures him, then, that he is a true Christian.

Paul lists gross sins that the legalists would condemn (sexual immorality, sensuality, sorcery, etc.), but follows them with the very sins (enmity, strife, jealousy, etc.) of which they were guilty of (v. 15).

verse_quote: will not inherit the kingdom of God.
note: One of eight occurrences of the phrase “kingdom of God” in the Pauline letters (also Rom. 14:17; 1 Cor. 4:20; 6:9, 10; 15:50; Col. 4:11; 2 Thess. 1:4; but cf. “kingdom of Christ and God” in Eph. 5:5). Paul’s point is that those who do not exhibit the graces of the Spirit (v. 22) in their lives will not take part in God’s eternal kingdom.

Paul uses the metaphor of fruit to describe the conduct of the believer in Rom. 6:22; Eph. 5:9; and Phil. 1:11. John the Baptist likewise claimed that true repentance would produce the “fruit” of concrete ethical behavior (Matt. 3:8; Luke 3:8); and Jesus promised that believers who draw life from Him, as branches united to the vine, will bear fruit that glorifies His Father (John 15:1–8). The love produced by the Spirit is like the love of Christ. It goes far beyond the performance of legalistic self-righteousness (Luke 10:25–37).

See 2:20; 6:14; Rom. 6:6. For the people of Christ, the cross broke the grip of the law (2:19) and also the grip of the flesh. By faith, they recognize the reality of their union with Christ in His death. So, too, they have been raised to new life in the Spirit of Christ and therefore walk in the Spirit (Col. 3:1, 3, 5).

Those who are in step with the Spirit (5:25) should reach out to the believer whom sin has ensnared, but they should be cautious lest sin also ensnare them in the process. Paul has said that every believer in Christ has been born of the Spirit (4:29) and received Him in fulfillment of God’s promise to Abraham (3:2–5, 14), so the responsibility to restore a fallen brother and sister belongs to all who are in Christ.

**spirit of gentleness.** Paul may mean an “attitude” of gentleness rather than harsh condemnation; but he also may imply that God’s Spirit, whose fruit includes gentleness (5:22), enables believers to restore one another.

Another Christian’s ensnarement in sin is not his private problem, but is a burden that others must bear with him and intervene to help him escape.

**the law of Christ.** This includes loving not only one’s neighbor (5:14; Matt. 22:39) but one’s enemy as well (Matt. 5:43, 44), with God’s love as the model.

Paul urges the Galatian Christians to examine themselves as individuals before God, rather than drawing false confidence from relative comparisons with others (cf. 2 Cor. 13:5, 6).

**reason to boast will be in himself.** Lit. “have reason to boast in himself.” As Paul subsequently makes clear, reason for “boasting” is not to be found in one’s obedience to the law. While the Judaizers “boasted” of their success in encouraging legalism (v. 13), Paul “boasts” in the cross of Christ alone (v. 14; cf. 2 Cor. 11:16–12:10). Paul’s meaning may be that encouragement over our progress in sanctification is to be derived not by comparing ourselves to others but by reviewing our growth from earlier immaturity, which the Spirit has granted.

This is a different Gk. word from the “burden” of v. 2, signaling a shift in the metaphor. Paul encouraged Christians to help others with the “burden” of overcoming temptation (v. 2). Here Paul means that we should not take pride in how much better we are than others, for God alone is our Judge.

verse_quote: share all good things with the one who teaches.
note: Although Paul did not always enforce his right to receive financial support from those whom he taught, he nonetheless contended that it was appropriate that “those who proclaim the gospel should get their living from the gospel” (1 Cor. 9:3–14).

Christians are called to help relieve the suffering of those outside its fellowship (Luke 10:25–37; cf. Lev. 19:10, 34; Deut. 14:29), but they have a special responsibility to help brothers and sisters in Christ who are in need (1 Thess. 3:12).

Paul sometimes dictated his letters to a secretary (Rom. 16:22) but customarily wrote the conclusion himself (1 Cor. 16:21; Col. 4:18; 2 Thess. 3:17). His “large letters” may mean that his eyesight was poor (4:15 note).

See note on 2:3.

**may not be persecuted.** It is possible that those advocating circumcision in Galatia were doing so under pressure from extremely zealous Jewish nationalists in Judea (4:17 note).

For a more detailed outworking of this concept, see 1 Cor. 1:18–2:5.

**the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.** Because Paul has been crucified with Christ (2:20), the criteria and approval of those who are outside Christ no longer define his identity and control his values.

See note on 5:6.

**a new creation.** The Holy Spirit’s activity in the believers’ lives reverses the effects of the fall and produces a renewed people (2 Cor. 5:17) who will eventually take their place in the new heaven and earth (Rev. 21:1). As in 2 Cor. 5:17, “new creation” here is to be viewed as the beginning fulfillment of the latter-day new creation prophecies of Is. 43:18, 19; 65:17; and 66:22.

This is a debated phrase among commentators. In view of Paul’s argument throughout the epistle that believers of every race are Abraham’s descendants (or “seed,” which is another phrase for true Israel) and heirs in Christ (who is “Abraham’s seed,” true Israel), this phrase probably refers to “those who walk by this rule” (the new creation that transcends the divide between circumcision and uncircumcision, and the faith that boasts in Christ’s cross; vv. 14, 15). Thus, “the Israel of God” is the newly constituted people of God composed of believing Gentiles and Jews (3:26–29), whose identifying mark is the Holy Spirit and not circumcision, (5:2–6; see Phil. 3:3). Some commentators see the phrase referring to the “fullness” of believing ethnic Israel, the elect of the Jewish nation for whose salvation Paul was deeply concerned (cf. Rom. 9:1–5; 11:12, 26, 31). In that case, Paul’s benediction implies his desire and hope for the “regrafting” of Jews into Christ by faith. This alternate interpretation is unlikely (cf. Rom. 11).

The Gk. word denotes the brands used to mark a slave as the property of a certain master. The word was also used to refer to the mark that pagan priests carried to identify the god they served. Paul uses the word to refer to the scars he received during his missionary activity (2 Cor. 11:23–25). These scars branded him as a slave of Christ (Rom. 1:1; Phil. 1:1; Titus 1:1).
A fitting conclusion to the letter in which Paul is most intensely concerned with God’s grace. The benediction summarizes Paul’s hope that among the Galatians the gospel of God’s grace will triumph.
